questions.questionText:
Indigenous Religion & Identity:
(a) State four titles/names used for the Supreme Being (Mwari) in Zimbabwean Indigenous Religion. [4 marks]
(b) Explain the importance of totems (mitupo/izibongo) in preserving family unity and nature conservation. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Musikavanhu, Nyadenga, Dzivaguru, Matangakugara, uMvelinqangi / uNkulunkulu [4].
(b) Totems build instant clan hospitality across strangers [2], prohibit incestuous marriage within same-totem clans [2], and deter killing/eating one's totem animal, protecting biodiversity [2].

questions.questionText:
Unhu / Ubuntu & Family Life:
(a) Define the concept of Unhu/Ubuntu. [2 marks]
(b) Discuss four ways extended families support vulnerable children and elderly relatives in Zimbabwe. [8 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) African moral philosophy stressing shared humanity, compassion, honesty, and respect ("Munhu munhu nekuda kwevanhu") [2].
(b) Absorbing orphans ("nhaka"/kinship fostering) instead of leaving them homeless [2]; pooling school fees/food in crises [2]; grandparents imparting moral wisdom & folklore [2]; caring physically for sick/elderly parents [2].

questions.questionText:
Christianity in Action:
(a) Outline Jesus' teaching on forgiveness as shown in a named parable (e.g., Unforgiving Servant or Prodigal Son). [4 marks]
(b) Suggest three ways Christian churches in Zimbabwe promote reconciliation after conflict. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) In the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), the father welcomes back his repentant wayward son with embrace and celebration rather than vengeance, teaching unlimited mercy [4].
(b) Mediating family/community disputes peacefully; pastoral counselling & forgiveness workshops; preaching national unity and anti-violence [6].

questions.questionText:
Islam — Beliefs & Practices:
(a) List the Five Pillars of Islam in English (or Arabic). [5 marks]
(b) Explain how Zakat and Sawm benefit both the individual believer and wider society. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (obligatory almsgiving), Sawm (Ramadan fasting), Hajj (Mecca pilgrimage) [5].
(b) Zakat redistributes wealth to relieve poverty and widows/orphans [2.5]; Sawm cultivates self-control and deepens empathy for the hungry, inspiring generosity [2.5].

questions.questionText:
Judaism:
(a) State four dietary laws/features of Kosher (Kashrut) eating in Judaism. [4 marks]
(b) Explain the religious significance of the Synagogue in Jewish community life. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Pork and shellfish are forbidden; land animals must chew cud and have split hooves; meat and dairy are never cooked/eaten together; slaughter must be humane (Shechita) [4].
(b) Serves as house of prayer (Bet Tefilah), Torah study school (Bet Midrash), and social welfare gathering centre (Bet Knesset) preserving identity [6].

questions.questionText:
Religion & Gender Equality:
(a) Identify three negative cultural or religious practices that have historically disadvantaged women/girls. [3 marks]
(b) Explain how modern religious teachings and Zimbabwean law promote gender equality in leadership and education. [7 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Child pledging/early marriage; unequal inheritance depriving widows; barring women from decision-making roles [3].
(b) Scripture affirms male and female created equally in God's image; Zimbabwe's Constitution criminalises child marriage and guarantees equal property/education access; many churches ordain women pastors and fund girls' STEM/leadership schooling [7].

questions.questionText:
Religion & Environmental Stewardship:
(a) Describe two traditional taboos/customs in Indigenous Religion that protect water sources or forests. [4 marks]
(b) Compare Christian and Islamic teachings on human stewardship of the Earth. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Sacred forests/burial hills (marinda) may not be cut for timber; forbidding soap washing or metal pots at sacred springs protects water purity [4].
(b) Genesis 2:15 tasks humans to "till and keep" creation responsibly; Qur'an appoints humanity as Khalifa (vicegerents/trustees) forbidden from spreading corruption/waste on Earth [6].

questions.questionText:
Religion, Health & Substance Abuse:
(a) State four causes of drug and substance abuse among school-going youth. [4 marks]
(b) Explain how religious values and community programmes can prevent youth substance abuse. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Peer pressure, family breakdown/trauma, idleness/unemployment, cheap illicit availability [4].
(b) Teaching body sanctity and self-discipline; vibrant youth choirs/sports clubs keeping youth constructively engaged; compassionate rehabilitation & peer mentoring without shaming [6].

questions.questionText:
Marriage & Family Responsibilities:
(a) State three causes of marital breakdown in contemporary society. [3 marks]
(b) Discuss four religious values that strengthen stable marriages. [7 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Infidelity, financial secrecy/irresponsibility, domestic violence, poor communication [3].
(b) Unconditional love and mutual respect; marital faithfulness; patient forgiveness; open joint financial planning and prayerful counsel [7].

questions.questionText:
Freedom of Worship & Religious Tolerance:
(a) Explain what religious pluralism means in Zimbabwe. [2 marks]
(b) Give four practical guidelines schools should follow to respect learners of different faiths (ATR, Christianity, Islam, Judaism). [8 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Coexistence of multiple diverse religions within one nation under equal constitutional protection [2].
(b) Respect dietary needs (halal/kosher/pork-free options); avoid mocking minority dress/headscarves; allow reasonable prayer accommodations; teach objective comparative religion fostering empathy [8].

questions.questionText:
Religion & Wealth/Work Ethics:
(a) Explain why hard honest work ("kushanda nesimba") is praised in Indigenous Religion and Christianity. [4 marks]
(b) Contrast ethical wealth creation with exploitation (e.g., underpaying workers or charging extortionate interest). [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Proverbs/Pauline teaching condemn laziness ("whoever refuses to work shall not eat"); ATR respects diligent farmers able to host nhimbe and feed orphans [4].
(b) Ethical enterprise creates fair jobs and honours contracts; exploitation harms families and violates scriptural justice ("do not withhold labourers' wages") [6].

questions.questionText:
Death, Bereavement & Afterlife:
(a) Briefly compare beliefs about life after death in Indigenous Religion and Christianity. [6 marks]
(b) State four ways a community shows Unhu during a neighbour's funeral (chema/kuchema). [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) In ATR, virtuous elders join ancestral spirits (vadzimu) watching over living kin; in Christianity, believers await resurrection and eternal communion with God while rejecting unrepentant sin [6].
(b) Contributing food/chema money; attending night vigil (bira/kuchema) to console bereaved; helping dig/prepare homestead; pausing field work in solidarity [4].

questions.questionText:
Rites of Passage:
(a) Define a "rite of passage" and list three stages of life marked by religious ceremonies. [4 marks]
(b) Describe how naming ceremonies in ATR and infant dedication/baptism in Christianity welcome a new child into community. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) A formal ceremony marking transition from one social/spiritual status to another: birth/naming, puberty/initiation, marriage, death [4].
(b) ATR naming connects child to clan ancestors and mutupo heritage; Christian baptism/dedication asks God's blessing and commits parents + congregation to raise the child morally [6].

questions.questionText:
Technology, Media & Morality:
Explain two ways digital media helps religious outreach today, and three moral dangers youths must guard against online. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Benefits: Livestreaming sermons to sick/diaspora members; digital sacred texts & study groups [2]. Dangers: Cyberbullying, pornography harming dignity, online gambling/scams, and spreading hate speech/false rumours [3].

questions.questionText:
Conflict Resolution:
Outline a five-step peaceful conflict resolution process informed by religious and Ubuntu principles when two neighbours dispute a boundary fence. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Calmly pause hostility and agree to meet with impartial elders/leaders [1]. 2. Allow each side uninterrupted fair hearing [1]. 3. Acknowledge wrongdoing sincerely without pride [1]. 4. Agree a fair restitution/boundary marker [1]. 5. Share goodwill/reconciliation restoring neighbourly harmony [1].

questions.questionText: Explain the role of religious Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) and faith-based schools/hospitals (e.g., mission hospitals) in Zimbabwe's national development. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Build and staff remote rural schools and mission clinics/hospitals (educating leaders and treating mothers/children) [2]; provide drought food aid, boreholes, and orphan scholarships [2]; run vocational carpentry/agriculture centres empowering youth [2].

questions.questionText: Compare the roles of a traditional healer (n'anga / inyanga) and a modern medical doctor, showing areas where safe cooperation helps public health. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: N'anga addresses perceived spiritual/ancestral disharmony and herbal remedies, whereas medical doctors diagnose biological pathogens/anatomy using scientific diagnostics & medicines [3]. Safe cooperation: traditional practitioners referring TB, malaria, HIV, and maternity emergencies promptly to clinics while preserving positive herbal research [2].

questions.questionText: Explain why "justice tempered with mercy" is vital in a school disciplinary committee dealing with a first-time student offender. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Fair rules deter misconduct and uphold accountability (justice) [2], while restorative counselling and second-chance community service rehabilitate the learner instead of permanently ruining their education (mercy) [3].

questions.questionText: Identify four moral qualities of a good citizen according to both the National Pledge/Constitution and religious ethics. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Honesty and rejection of bribery. 2. Respect for human life and property. 3. Tolerance across ethnic/religious differences. 4. Diligent stewardship of public resources and care for the vulnerable [4 marks].

questions.questionText: Explain what "nhimbe / ilima" is in Zimbabwean culture and discuss three social and economic benefits it brings to rural villages. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Nhimbe/ilima is communal cooperative labour where neighbours help each other clear fields, weed, harvest, or roof huts in exchange for shared food/maheu [2]. Benefits: finishes heavy farm tasks on time for widows/elderly; prevents starvation; strengthens lifelong village solidarity [3].
